newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Royal, Scotia banks in takeover moves.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Royal, Scotia banks in takeover moves.

text.p: Two of Canada's big six banks took steps on Tuesday to tighten their grip on the country's trust company business and secure access to the insurance industry.
Bank of Nova Scotia offered to acquire Toronto-based National Trustco Co., Canada's last big family-owned trust, in a cash and stock deal valued at C$1.25 billion ($898 million).
Meanwhile, one of Canada's biggest insurers, London Insurance Group said it was in talks to be acquired by Canada's biggest bank, Royal Bank of Canada.
Analysts saw the moves as bids by the banks to expand beyond the traditional banking and brokerage businesses that Canada's major banks dominate.

"They are getting tapped out in Canada," said Kent Wideman, senior vice president at Dominion Bond Rating Service. "The banks albeit big here, are not big on a global scale and in fact they've been falling in recent years."

Analysts said the combination of Scotiabank and National Trustco would strengthen Scotiabank's domestic operations, which have lagged as it focused on expanding its assets outside Canada, where 41 percent of its assets are now based.
The analysts said the acquisition would also make Scotiabank less of a takeover target in the event that the Canadian government repealed legislation banning bank takeovers.
Scotiabank said it would offer 0.125 of a common share plus C$26.475 ($19.04) cash for each common share of National Trustco.

The bank said it already owned 2.4 percent of National Trustco and had lockup agreements for 47 percent of the company's outstanding common shares. The offer would be available to shareholders until July 31.
National Trustco Chairman Hal Jackman told a news conference that the deal was not open to competing bids.
Analysts said that Royal Bank, meanwhile, would take a big leap into the insurance business if it acquired London Insurance, which has Canada's top market share in individual life insurance.
Analysts said Royal's interest in London came in anticipation that Canadian banks would soon be permitted to sell insurance through their branches, using their bank client lists.
"Those are the two things that they haven't got at this point," Wideman said. "Banks might value the latter even more than the former if they can target market it (insurance)."
The federal government is currently reviewing rules that block banks from selling insurance in their branches or using their client lists for such sales.
Most major Canadian trust companies -- the equivalent of U.S. savings and loans -- have been gobbled up by the banks.

But the largest Canadian insurers remain either units of foreign insurance companies or independent companies. They have lobbied the government hard against allowing the banks to use their branches and client lists for selling insurance.

Wideman said the Royal Bank-London talks "may throw another interesting wrench into the whole aspect because London was one of the companies that was one of the most powerful in lobbying against all this."

Royal Bank declined to comment on the talks, but analysts said the bank may have been surprised by London's statement, which followed a report on Tuesday about the talks in Toronto's Globe and Mail newspaper.
"It could be the beginning of a bidding process," Maxwell said.
London shares rose C$2.80 to C$26.30 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday, while Royal Bank gained C$1.15 to C$63.15.
National Trustco shares rose C$6.60 to C$33.35 in Toronto, while Scotiabank was up C$2.25 to C$60.05.
